results.claim: FLEX led to the discovery of a cool flame: the fuel kept burning under certain conditions after the visible flame went out.
results.quote: FLEX, which analyzed the effectiveness of fire suppressants, led to the discovery of a type of cool flame, where the fuel continued "burning" under certain conditions after extinction of the visible flame.

results.claim: As the opposed flow was gradually reduced, the thin-film flame shrank, lost its orange color and became completely blue.
results.quote: As the flow speed is gradually reduced from about t = 27 s, the flame size starts shrinking and the orange color disappears and the flame becomes completely blue, most possibly because of the temperature drop brought about by radiative losses, which is enhanced by the increased residence time at low flow velocity.

results.claim: Just before quenching the rod flame shrank to a hemispherical blue shape, and pre-quenching oscillations at 1.1 Hz were observed with a radiometer.
results.quote: The flame shrinks to a hemispherical blue shape just before quenching. Prequenching extinction oscillations at 1.1 Hz are observed with a radiometer and are similar to previously reported quiescent candle flame oscillations in microgravity.

results.claim: In the concurrent rod tests CO production increased significantly at low O2 levels, and so did the CO to CO2 ratio.
results.quote: CO production also increases significantly at low O2 levels. The CO to CO2 ratio increases as well at low O2 concentrations.

results.claim: At very low flow velocities the rod flames appeared very small, blue, faint and open at their downstream ends; as flow rose toward 20 mm/s and above they became much more luminous, with bright yellow flames.
results.quote: Visually it was observed that at very low flow velocities the flames appear to be very small, blue, faint, and open at their downstream ends. As the flow velocity rises towards 20 mm/s and above, the flames become much more luminous, with bright yellow flames, and a closed downstream tip.

results.claim: CO to CO2 ratios for the BASS-II fires were an order of magnitude higher than for efficient flue gases.
results.quote: The CO to CO2 ratios for these fires are an order of magnitude higher than for efficient flue gases, indicating that these flames are not efficient.

results.claim: Concurrent-flow PMMA rod flames produced on average 550 ppm of CO for every 1 percent of CO2.
results.quote: Figure 1.4 shows that the concurrent rods produced on average 550 ppm of CO for every 1 percent of CO2.

results.claim: In general the BASS-II flames were under-ventilated and did not burn all of the vaporized fuel: some ended up as soot, some as CO and some as unburned hydrocarbons.
results.quote: So, in general, the flames were under- ventilated and did not burn all of the vaporized fuel. Some fuel ended up as soot, some as CO, and some as unburned hydrocarbons.

results.claim: When flow speed and oxygen concentration were low the fabric flame became very dim blue and was difficult to see in the side video camera.
results.quote: When flow speed and oxygen concentration were low, the flame became very dim blue and was difficult to see in the side video camera.

results.claim: Quench test burns on PMMA rods lasted up to 28 minutes.
results.quote: Quench test burns lasted up to 28 minutes.

results.claim: SAME-R baseline runs (geometric mean / count mean / diameter of average mass, micrometers; geometric standard deviation). Unaged: Kapton 0.047/0.062/0.106 (2.072), lampwick 0.103/0.142/0.271 (2.232), silicone 0.152/0.221/0.468 (2.382), Teflon 0.093/0.111/0.173 (2.081), Pyrell 0.177/0.227/0.377 (2.032). Aged 720 s: Kapton 0.102/0.121/0.169 (1.790), lampwick 0.269/0.308/0.401 (1.673), silicone 0.320/0.400/0.628 (1.956), Teflon 0.080/0.115/0.237 (2.342), Pyrell 0.348/0.400/0.529 (1.697).

For Teflon, Kapton and lampwick, particle size plotted against duct velocity shows a strong trend of larger particles at low flow rates; the report concludes that smoke trapped in an avionics enclosure can be expected to be substantially larger than smoke released in ventilated areas.
results.quote: The results for Teflon, Kapton and lampwick are plotted versus duct velocity in figures 6, 7 and 8. These figures show a strong trend of increased particle size at low flow rates. This indicates that smoke trapped in an avionics enclosure can be expected to be substantially larger than smoke released in ventilated areas.

results.claim: For all materials the diameter of average mass was 30% to 40% larger in the zero-flow tests than in the tests with flow.
results.quote: It is found for all of the materials the diameter of average mass is 30 % to 40 % larger for the zero-flow tests compared to the flow tests.

results.claim: The conclusions of the SAME-R final report state that the zero-flow conditions produced smoke particles 2 to 3 times larger than those produced at the nominal 8 cm/s flow rate.
results.quote: The zero flow conditions produced smoke particles that were 2 to 3 times larger than those produced at the nominal 8 cm/s flow rate.

results.claim: The report stresses that the zero-flow condition is unique to low gravity: at 1-g the buoyancy of the rising gases would greatly increase the mixing zone, so the larger particles seen at zero flow matter for the design of fire detection equipment for space vehicles.
results.quote: It is important to recognize that this condition is unique to low-gravity scenarios. If one performed the same experiment at 1-g, the buoyancy of the rising gases would greatly increase the mixing zone. So the larger particle diameters observed in these zero-flow conditions are important to consider in the development of improved fire detection equipment for space vehicles.

results.claim: Pyrell smoke changed from fractal-like clusters of up to 30 primary spheres at 8 cm/s air flow to spherical particles at zero flow.
results.quote: the change in the morphology of the Pyrell smoke from fractal-like clusters with up to 30 primary spheres for the case with a flow of 8 cm/s to spherical particles for the zero-flow condition

results.claim: All samples produced significant numbers of sub-micron particles that are readily detected by an ionization smoke detector, but the aging results suggest that some materials, such as silicone rubber, can produce smoke that reaches sizes better detected by light scattering.
results.quote: all samples produced significant numbers of sub-micron particulate that are readily detected using an ionization smoke detector. However, the aging results suggest that some materials such as silicone rubber can produce smoke that can reach sizes better detected by light scattering techniques.

results.claim: The SAME-R conclusions suggest that detection methods measuring more than one moment of the size distribution may detect better and reject false alarms better than single-moment detectors.
results.quote: These results suggest that detection methods that can measure more than one moment of the size distribution may show more successful detection and false alarm rejection than single moment detectors.

results.claim: By combining two moments, the MPASS prototype can tell a strong signal from a high smoke concentration apart from a strong signal from a lower concentration of very large dust particles, which can minimize false smoke detector alarms.
results.quote: The MPASS therefore has the ability to discern the difference between a strong signal from a high smoke concentration and a strong signal from a lower concentration of very large dust particles, a feature which can minimize false smoke detector alarms.

results.claim: Using a correlation of two measured moments reduced the relative variance of the MPASS response by roughly a factor of at least 2 compared with a conventional single-output sensor.
results.quote: Both figures show that the correlation decreases the relative variance by roughly a factor of at least 2 relative to that provided by a conventional single-output sensor.

results.claim: Silicone rubber smoke left no particles visible by TEM, presumably because the particles were condensed liquid that evaporated before they could be imaged.
results.quote: Overall, silicone rubber presented no particles that were visible via TEM, presumably because the particles were condensed liquid that evaporated before they could be imaged in the TEM.

results.claim: The report describes coagulation as continuing for time scales of up to a thousand seconds and states that liquid particles coalesce into larger droplets, which is the case for the lampwick, silicone rubber and Kapton smokes (Fig. 11).
results.quote: This process may continue for time scales of up to thousand seconds. If the particles are liquid, the colliding particles will coalesce and form larger droplets. This is the case for the lampwick, silicone rubber, and Kapton smokes (Fig. 11).

results.claim: For the same heater setting (wire resistance ratio Rt/R0) the actual sample heating temperature differed by as much as 30 degrees Celsius between tests.
results.quote: for the same Rt/R0, the actual heating temperature difference can be as large as 30 degrees Celsius

results.claim: Morphology results show that only Kapton and lamp wick are spherical aerosols, so they are better suited to the moment method.
results.quote: Morphology results show that only Kapton and lamp wick are spherical aerosols so they are better suited to the moment method.

results.claim: From the SAME-R flight and ground tests the team concluded that the moment method, together with the lognormal distribution assumption, is a valid and effective way to characterize aerosols encountered in space vehicles.
results.quote: it is concluded that the moment method in conjunction the lognormal distribution assumption is a valid and effective approach to characterization of the aerosol encountered in space vehicles.
